title: Scale and proportion — Image Wiki
text:
Scale and proportion
  Scale is how big something looks compared with something you already know. Proportion is how the parts of one thing relate to each other. They share a word and almost nothing else.

  
    Termscale and proportion
    Also calledsense of scale, relative size, ratio, canon of proportions
    Not the same assize in pixels, focal length, the golden ratio as a rule
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why a picture can tell you how big something isBreaking it on purposeProportion is the other thingAbout the golden ratioCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Geologists put a hammer in the frame. Divers lay a ruler beside the wreck. Nobody thinks the hammer is interesting — but a photograph of a rock with nothing else in it cannot tell you whether the rock is the size of a fist or of a house, and no amount of sharpness will fix that.
Scale is how big a thing looks relative to something you already know. It is a relationship, not a property of the object, and if the picture does not supply the other end of it the reading is unavailable.
Proportion is the relation of parts within one thing: head to body, window to wall, sleeve to torso. Different question, same word in English.
Why a picture can tell you how big something is


No reference object: the pillars could be two metres or twenty
One human figure on the ridge, and the pillars are settled


Rock pillars (kigilyakh) of the Ulakhan-Sis range, Sakha, northern Siberia. Photograph by Artem Abdukakharov via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. The left panel is our own crop of the same photograph, taken from the left of the frame; nothing else was changed.
Left. Try to say how tall these are. You cannot, and the frustrating part is that nothing is missing — the rock is sharp, well lit, and clearly described. The lichen and the loose blocks in the foreground hint at a metre or so, so most people guess low: garden boulders, a stone circle, a few metres at most.
Right. One person, standing on the ridge to the right, and the guess collapses into a fact. The pillars are roughly ten times a person, so somewhere in the region of fifteen metres — five storeys of rock. Nothing about the stone changed between the two panels. Your knowledge of how tall people are did the entire job.



about 2 m tall1.7 mReference figure close to the rockthe rock is barely taller than a personabout 15 m tall1.7 mReference figure small in the framethe same rock is a five-storey cliffThe rock is the same size in pixels in both panels. Only the figure changed.

The rock is drawn at exactly the same pixel size in both panels. The only variable is the height of the person beside it.
Because you know a person is about 1.7 m, you divide: rock height ÷ figure height × 1.7. On the left the arithmetic gives about two metres, and the rock reads as something you could climb onto. On the right the same outline works out at about fifteen metres, and it reads as a cliff. The picture never states a size. It states a ratio, and you supply the unit.


Four things can supply that unit, roughly in order of reliability:

A familiar object. A person, a car, a doorway, a coin, a boot. A human figure is strongest, because your estimate of human height is unusually tight.
Texture that gets finer with distance. Cobbles, furrows, waves, tree crowns: if a repeating element shrinks steadily across the frame, its size at the front is a ruler for the front. One of the standard Depth cues.
Haze. Distant things go paler and bluer, and heavy haze means kilometres, not metres. Smarthistory tracks it in Perugino as a deliberate device (SRC-009); see Atmospheric perspective.
Detail falling off. Past some distance you stop seeing individual leaves, bricks or faces, and where that cut-off lands says roughly how far away you are.

Remove all four and scale goes free. That is why a well-photographed architectural model reads as a building. No craft fooled you; you were never given the comparison, so your visual system assumed the thing was the size such things usually are.



Albert Bierstadt, The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak, 1863 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain.
All four cues at once, on purpose. The bottom fifth of the canvas is an encampment: tipis, horses, dogs, dozens of people. Measure one standing figure against the waterfall behind it, then against the snowfield above that, and the mountain sizes itself.
The long distances are carried by the other three. The peaks are pale, blue and almost without detail, while the foreground grass has individual blades; the trees on the middle ridges are separate crowns at the near edge and an even nap at the far one.
Cover the encampment with your hand. The picture still reads as mountains — but as mountains of no particular size, and most of its drama leaves with the horses.


Breaking it on purpose
Because scale is a relationship, you can set it to whatever you like. Cooper Hewitt lists manipulate scale among the fourteen moves a poster can make: exaggerate the size difference to force depth, or put a giant head beside a tiny figure in the same flat rectangle (POST-001-SUP1). A face three metres wide is not a big face — it is a different kind of object, and the rest of the poster becomes its thoughts.
Proportion is the other thing
Proportion asks how the parts of one object relate, and unlike scale it can be judged with no external reference at all (SRC-001).
Vitruvius wrote a canon for the human figure in plain whole-number fractions — the face a tenth of the height, the head an eighth, the foot a sixth — and Leonardo drew it out. Figure drawing still uses the same kind of shorthand: about seven and a half head-heights to a standing adult, eight for a heroic one. These are averages, and their value is diagnostic. When a figure looks wrong and you cannot say why, counting heads usually finds it.



Leonardo da Vinci, Vitruvian Man, c. 1490 (Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice). Public domain.
A drawing about proportion and nothing else, and there is no reference object anywhere in it — which is the point. Everything here is a comparison of one part of the body with another part.
Look at the two enclosing figures. The square works because the arm span equals the standing height; put your fingers on the fingertips and the toes and you can check it. The circle is centred not on the chest but on the navel, and it is the arms-raised, legs-apart pose that touches it. Two different claims about the same body, drawn on top of each other.
Then look for the measuring apparatus. There is a graduated bar under the feet, and short tick marks across the forearms and along the raised arms. Leonardo is dividing the figure into named fractions, exactly as Vitruvius specified them — and the fractions are plain ones: a tenth, an eighth, a sixth. No irrational numbers were required.


About the golden ratio
You will meet the claim that one number, φ = 1.618…, governs beautiful proportion. The number is real and so is the geometry: cut a square off a rectangle with those sides and the leftover has the same ratio again, forever. That property is why the shape recurs in decorative systems.

square1 : 1.618again11.6180Golden rectanglecut off a square and the leftover is golden tooA51 : 1.414A51 : 1.41411.4142ISO A rectanglefold it in half and the halves are A-shaped tooA4 is 210 x 297 mm, so 297 / 210 = 1.414. It is not a golden rectangle.

Two self-similar rectangles that are routinely confused. Left, the golden rectangle: take a square off the end and the remainder is golden again. Right, the ISO A rectangle: fold it in half and each half has the same proportion, which is what lets A4 become two A5s.
They are not the same shape and not the same number. Golden is 1 : 1.618; the A series is 1 : √2 = 1 : 1.414. A4 is 210 × 297 mm, and 297 ÷ 210 = 1.414.


The distinction is worth having, because respectable sources get it wrong. The Vignelli Canon — a good book by a great designer — states that the international A paper sizes are "based on a golden rectangle, the divine proportion" (LAY-001). They are not. They are built on √2 so that halving preserves the proportion, which is why two A5 sheets tile an A4.
On aesthetics, be careful in both directions. Preference experiments go back to Fechner in the 1860s, and people asked to pick a favourite rectangle do cluster somewhere near 1.6. Christopher Green's review of a century of that work (Perception, 1995) concluded the effect is probably real but fragile — easily manufactured or destroyed by how the experiment is run. The historical claims are worse off: the Parthenon, the pyramids, the Mona Lisa. George Markowsky went through them in The College Mathematics Journal in 1992 and found the measurements picked to fit.
So: a real number, a long decorative history, wobbly evidence about bare rectangles, and no evidence that a picture divided on golden proportions is preferred to one divided some other way. Use it if you like the shape; do not use it as an argument, and never mark an image down for missing it. Same position the wiki takes on the rule of thirds. For ratios that earn their keep, see Grids.
Common mistakes

"This object is out of scale." Usually you mean it is the wrong size relative to its neighbours. Say that instead; it is checkable.
"No sense of scale, so add a person." A person also adds a subject, a face and a story. A boot or a doorway is often the cheaper fix.
"Big means important." Size is one pull among several and weak on its own; a small dark thing beats a large pale one. See Visual hierarchy.
"Proportion means the golden ratio." It means the relations of the parts, and the useful canons are simple fractions: halves, thirds, head-heights.
"You cannot fake scale in a photograph." You can, by removing every reference — which is also how a tight crop destroys it by accident.


Reading scale in an image

Name the one object in the frame whose real size you know.
If there is none, say so — and treat any size you had in mind as your assumption, not the picture's claim.
Measure the subject against that reference in units of it: "about three doors tall".
Check the cues agree. A figure saying ten metres and haze saying ten kilometres means a composite or a perspective error.
For proportion, ignore everything outside the object. Count heads, or compare a part against the whole.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Depth cues
              A picture is a flat surface. It reads as deep because a dozen separate cues all point the same way, and your eye believes the majority.
            
          
        
          
            
              Grids
              A set of decisions taken once — margins, columns, gutters, modules, baselines — so that no later page needs a fresh decision. It is a system, not a look.
            
          
        
          
            
              Rhythm and repetition
              Repeating something turns many things into one thing — and the moment it does, whatever does not belong to the set becomes impossible to miss.
            
          
        
          
            
              Atmospheric perspective
              Distant things go pale, flat and sky-coloured because you are looking at them through more air, and air scatters light.
